_about: Plain-English renderings for the medicine and psychiatry shelves. Same rules as plain_english.json. Trial results are stated as the paper reports them; none of this is medical advice.
10.2105/ajph.2025.308244: Flint, Michigan runs Rx Kids, which gives every pregnant resident and new parent cash with no conditions attached. Comparing Flint mothers who gave birth before and after it started with mothers outside the city, the researchers found a 4.2-point drop in the risk of eviction and a 14-point drop in screening positive for postpartum depression. Mothers also reported more trust in institutions and more sense of being valued.
10.2105/ajph.2025.308289: Texas banned abortion after about six weeks in 2021 and then entirely after Dobbs in 2022. Using records from every Texas hospital and surgical facility, the authors counted blood transfusions during pregnancy loss - a marker of dangerous bleeding. Under the six-week ban the numbers looked normal; under the total ban there were about 51 more transfusions per quarter than history predicted, a 15 percent rise.
10.2105/ajph.2025.308277: A federally funded programme in south central Texas set out to counter COVID-19 misinformation in communities that official messaging was not reaching. Rather than broadcasting, it gathered data with the community and pushed health information through partners people already trusted, tailoring the message culturally. The authors report the collaborations and the trust outlasted the programme.
10.2105/ajph.2025.308265: The authors place the 2025 executive orders restricting gender-affirming care in a longer history of medicine treating transgender bodies as pathology and of doctors acting as gatekeepers. They document what the orders get scientifically wrong, trace the effects of related legislation including United States v Skrmetti, and argue the restrictions cut against clinicians' duty to provide evidence-based care.
10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.1674: Some people with psychosis do not respond to antipsychotics, and there is no way to tell in advance. Pooling the raw participant data from eighteen brain-chemistry imaging studies plus five more by summary, this analysis looked for chemical markers that distinguish responders from non-responders - the kind of evidence that could eventually support predicting who will respond and finding new drug targets.
10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.1078: Mental illness comes in degrees, but clinical decisions are yes-or-no: treat or wait, fund or decline, enrol or don't. This review compares the strategies for drawing the line - by diagnosis, by statistical deviance from the population, by actual functional impairment, and by the health-economics approach of asking where treatment starts paying off - and argues that the diagnosis-based default is the wrong tool for many of the decisions it is used for.
10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.1053: Inflammation has long been suspected as a cause of depression, but almost nobody has tested it by blocking inflammation directly. In this four-week placebo-controlled trial, adults whose depression had resisted antidepressants and who had raised inflammatory markers received a drug that inhibits interleukin 6. The study was designed to find which symptoms shift and by how much, to size a full trial rather than settle the question.
10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.1064: Psychiatric risk comes both from rare, large genetic deletions and duplications and from the accumulation of many common variants. Using Danish neonatal blood samples linked to every hospital diagnosis for people born between 1981 and 2008, this study estimates the absolute risk each carries for ADHD, autism, schizophrenia and depression - and, for the first time, what happens when someone has both.
10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.1752: Using Finnish registers covering everyone born between 1985 and 2000, the authors asked whether teenagers who are surrounded by peers with mental illness - or by peers who carry genetic risk for it - are themselves more likely to be diagnosed later. Peer groups were defined four ways, from school class up to postal code, which lets them separate genuine peer influence from simply living in the same place.
10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.1100: Brain imaging is everywhere in psychiatric research but rarely shown to improve outcomes. Accelerated TMS for treatment-resistant depression is now FDA-cleared using individualised, scan-guided targeting. This blinded trial in 40 adults compared that against the cheap alternative - measuring from the scalp - to find out whether the imaging is doing any work.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)00717-8: Polycystic ovary syndrome affects one woman in eight, and the name is wrong: there are no pathological cysts, and it obscures the hormonal and metabolic problems that actually define the condition. This paper reports the global process that renamed it polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, drawing on surveys of 14,360 patients and clinicians worldwide, 56 organisations, and formal consensus methods.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)00202-3: Orforglipron is a GLP-1 drug in pill form that, unlike existing oral options, does not need to be taken on an empty stomach with water restrictions. This 52-week phase 3 trial across five countries tested it head-to-head against oral semaglutide in adults with type 2 diabetes not controlled by metformin, asking whether it is no worse at lowering long-term blood sugar.
10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01565-x: The first of a three-part Lancet series tests the case against ultra-processed food. It finds the evidence supports all three claims: this pattern of eating is displacing traditional whole-food diets worldwide; it degrades diet quality, partly by driving overeating through energy density, hyper-palatability and soft texture; and it raises the risk of multiple chronic diseases.
10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01566-1: The second paper in the series sets out what governments could actually do. Existing policy targets fat, sugar and salt; the authors argue that is too narrow and propose measures across four fronts - the products themselves, the environments they are sold in, the manufacturers and retailers behind them, and the supply chains that make them cheap.
10.1016/s0140-6736(25)02105-1: A review of what the GLP-1 drugs have turned out to do beyond lowering blood sugar. They cut major cardiovascular events and heart-failure hospitalisations, reduce albuminuria and slow kidney decline, and - now approved for obesity - prevent type 2 diabetes, help heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and reverse fatty liver disease.
10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01567-3: The third paper argues the ultra-processed food industry is itself the driver, because these products are more profitable than the alternatives, which funds further expansion. It documents how the industry blocks regulation through a transnational network of front groups, multi-stakeholder initiatives and research partnerships, and draws the parallel with tobacco control.
10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01942-7: A clinical overview of chronic kidney disease, which now affects roughly 850 million people and is on track to be the world's fifth leading cause of death by 2050. The key clinical point: most patients die of cardiovascular disease before their kidneys ever fail. Since 2019 several large trials have found treatments that both slow kidney decline and cut cardiovascular risk.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01009-3: Finerenone is known to protect the kidneys in people whose chronic kidney disease comes from type 2 diabetes. Pooling the individual participant data from three randomised placebo-controlled trials, this analysis asks whether the benefit holds across other causes of kidney disease and across the range of kidney function and protein leakage.
10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01385-6: A practical update on osteoporosis, which the authors note is both very common in old age and badly undertreated despite effective drugs being available. It covers who to screen, how to assess fracture risk, and how to treat the very old, people with kidney disease, and people who keep fracturing anyway - with particular attention to stopping denosumab safely.
10.1016/s2215-0366(26)00090-8: People with psychosis often also have PTSD, and it makes their prognosis worse, but trauma therapy is frequently withheld from them on safety grounds. This trial across five UK sites randomly assigned adults with both conditions to nine months of trauma-focused therapy woven into standard CBT for psychosis, or to usual care alone, measuring PTSD severity at four and nine months.
10.1016/s2215-0366(26)00153-7: Lithium can be taken once or twice a day, and both work, but once-daily dosing produces bigger swings in the blood. Whether the brain sees those swings was unknown. Using lithium-7 MRI to scan the brain three times across a ten-hour day alongside matched blood samples, this study measured what the brain actually receives under each schedule.
10.1016/s2215-0366(25)00398-0: Young people with psychosis are at high risk of diabetes and heart disease, partly from the medication, and clinicians have had no reliable way to identify who. Using UK primary and secondary care records, the authors refined and validated a risk calculator for 16-to-35-year-olds and took it through to a regulated medical device rather than leaving it as a published model.
10.1016/s2215-0366(26)00060-x: Magnetic seizure therapy induces a seizure like ECT but more focally, with the hope of fewer memory side effects. This double-blind trial at three centres in Canada and the USA tested whether it is no worse than the gentlest effective form of ECT, using two co-primary outcomes: remission from depression, and loss of autobiographical memory.
10.1016/s2215-0366(26)00087-8: Reviewing cannabis policy changes worldwide from 2000 to 2025, the authors find commercial legalisation in Canada and the US was followed by more cannabis use, more cannabis use disorder and higher potency, plus more hospital admissions for psychosis - though no consistent rise in psychotic disorders overall. Tightly regulated legalisation showed weaker associations, which is the paper's central policy point.
10.1016/s2215-0366(26)00054-4: Anxiety and depression keep rising while treatment services run out of capacity. The authors argue that music, visual art, dance, creative writing and going to cultural events work on the same underlying processes as formal therapy - and share its contextual ingredients too, such as relationship, expectancy and identity - which is a reason to take them seriously alongside treatment rather than instead of it.
10.1056/nejmoa2605555: More than 90 percent of pancreatic cancers are driven by a mutated RAS gene, long considered undruggable. Daraxonrasib is an oral drug that locks onto the active form of RAS. In this phase 3 trial, 500 patients whose metastatic pancreatic cancer had already progressed on treatment were randomly assigned to it or to the oncologist's choice of chemotherapy, with survival as the primary measure.
10.1056/nejmsa2514268: After changes to the US vaccine advisory process disrupted official guidance, this team did the evidence review independently. Screening 17,263 references down to 511 studies, they found COVID-19 mRNA vaccines against the XBB.1.5 subvariant were about 46 to 50 percent effective at preventing hospitalisation in adults, and report the corresponding figures for RSV and influenza.
10.1056/nejmoa2515131: Hepatitis B can be suppressed but rarely cured. Bepirovirsen is an antisense drug that targets the virus's transcripts. Across two identical trials, patients on stable antiviral therapy received 24 weeks of bepirovirsen or placebo and then stopped their usual drugs. About 20 percent achieved a functional cure at 72 weeks - against none at all in the placebo groups.
10.1056/nejmoa2604625: Finerenone protects the kidneys in people with diabetes-related kidney disease. This trial asked whether it also helps people who have chronic kidney disease without diabetes, randomly assigning adults with reduced kidney function and protein in the urine to the drug or placebo and tracking how fast their kidney function declined over 32 months.
10.1056/nejmoa2503223: The European prostate screening trial started in 1993 and this is its final analysis, following 162,236 men aged 55 to 69 for a median of 23 years. Screening cut prostate cancer deaths by 13 percent - but the absolute reduction was 0.22 percent, which is the number that matters for anyone weighing a PSA test against the overdiagnosis it causes.
10.1056/nejmoa2514663: Teclistamab is a bispecific antibody that grabs a T cell with one arm and a myeloma cell with the other. In this phase 3 trial, 587 patients with relapsed multiple myeloma who had had one to three prior treatments received it with daratumumab, or a standard daratumumab combination. At 34.5 months, 83.4 percent were alive without progression versus 29.7 percent.
10.1056/nejmoa2509688: If catheter ablation has successfully stopped someone's atrial fibrillation, do they still need lifelong blood thinners? This international trial randomly assigned 1,284 such patients, all at some stroke risk, to aspirin or rivaroxaban for three years, with brain MRI at the start and end so that silent strokes were counted alongside obvious ones.
10.1056/nejmoa2511885: After bladder cancer surgery, some patients relapse and some are cured, and there is no good way to tell them apart. This trial monitored 761 patients for tumour DNA circulating in the blood; the 250 whose blood turned positive were randomly assigned to immunotherapy or placebo, while those who stayed negative were spared treatment altogether.
10.1056/nejmoa2514428: Evolocumab is known to prevent repeat heart attacks and strokes. This trial tested it in 12,257 people who had never had either but did have atherosclerosis or diabetes and high LDL cholesterol, randomly assigning them to the drug or placebo - the question being whether aggressive cholesterol lowering pays off before the first event rather than after.
